Static drawdown.long:
A static maximum loss level is fixed at the account's starting balance and never moves. On a 50,000 account with a 2,000 static limit, the floor sits at 48,000 on the first day and on the last, no matter whether the account has since traded up to 60,000.

The practical consequence is that room grows with profit. A trader who builds a 5,000 cushion under a static floor is now 7,000 from failure, and every winning day genuinely reduces the chance of being closed out. That is how most people intuitively assume a loss limit works.

It is also why static floors are the minority offering. From the firm's side, a static limit means a trader who gets lucky early can then take much larger swings while still technically inside the rules, and the firm's own exposure widens exactly when the trader's behaviour becomes least predictable.

Where people get fooled: assuming any advertised maximum loss is static because that is the intuitive reading. Most retail funded accounts trail the floor instead, and the difference between the two is far larger than the headline numbers suggest. The word to look for in the terms is not the size of the limit but whether it moves.
Static drawdown.usage: Described as a fixed loss floor that stays at the starting balance regardless of profits made.

Drawdown lock.long:
On a trailing account the loss floor follows equity upward. The lock is the point at which it stops following. Most commonly the floor trails until it reaches the original starting balance and then freezes there, so the account can no longer be failed while it is still in profit overall.

Where that lock sits is one of the most consequential numbers in the contract and one of the least advertised. A floor that locks at breakeven means the account becomes genuinely safer once the trader is a few thousand ahead. A floor that locks only at starting balance plus a buffer takes longer to reach. A floor that never locks keeps tightening for the life of the account.

The difference is not cosmetic. Under a never-locking floor, an account that has run up and given back is operating on a much shorter leash than its balance implies, and the trader usually discovers this at the worst moment.

Where people get fooled: reading the drawdown size and stopping there. Two accounts advertising the same maximum loss can behave completely differently depending on where and whether the floor locks, and that detail often sits several clicks deep in the terms rather than on the pricing page.
Drawdown lock.usage: Referred to when explaining at what point a trailing loss floor stops moving upward.

Instant funding.long:
Instant funding removes the evaluation phase. The fee buys a simulated account immediately, with loss rules attached and a profit share from the first trade, and there is no profit target to clear before withdrawals become possible.

The evaluation has not really been removed, though. It has been moved. The daily loss limit and the maximum drawdown still decide whether the account survives, and they still do the same filtering job the two-phase version did — just without a defined finish line to reach first. What changes is the order of events, not the selection mechanism.

The pricing reflects that. Instant accounts typically cost considerably more up front for the same nominal size, and frequently carry a worse profit split, tighter loss limits, or a lower payout ceiling than the equivalent evaluation product from the same firm. The firm is pricing the removed filter back in.

Where people get fooled: reading "no challenge" as "no test". The test is the loss rules, which were always the part that ended most accounts. Paying more to skip a profit target while keeping the limits that actually do the failing is a poor trade for anyone whose difficulty was the limits.
Instant funding.usage: Used for funded-account products sold without an evaluation phase, where trading begins immediately on payment.

Futures prop vs CFD prop.long:
Funded-account providers split into two families with genuinely different plumbing. Futures programmes sit on exchange-traded contracts — CME products such as the E-mini and Micro indices — where there is one central order book, one public tape, and central clearing. CFD and forex programmes sit on off-exchange contracts for difference, where pricing is decentralised and each provider's feed is its own.

The difference that matters is verifiability. On a futures programme, the price you were filled at can be checked against exchange data that the firm does not control. On a CFD programme the firm frequently is the counterparty to its own funded accounts, sets the feed, and may simulate fills entirely — so a disputed fill has no independent record to appeal to.

The secondary differences follow from that: futures programmes carry exchange data fees and platform requirements, while CFD programmes are cheaper to enter, run on familiar retail platforms, and market far more aggressively.

Where people get fooled: comparing the two on account size and profit split, which are the numbers both advertise, while ignoring that one has an independent price record and the other does not. That distinction only becomes visible in a dispute, which is precisely when it cannot be fixed.
Futures prop vs CFD prop.usage: Used to distinguish exchange-based futures funding programmes from off-exchange CFD and forex ones.

Payout compliance review.long:
When a funded trader requests a withdrawal, the firm audits the account. That review is not limited to the period the profit was made in — it typically re-examines the entire trading history, from the first order onward, against every rule in the agreement.

This is the structural asymmetry of the whole model. Rules are enforced retrospectively, at the exact moment money is claimed, rather than at the moment they are broken. A position held thirty seconds into a restricted news window in the first week does not stop the account then. It surfaces months later as grounds to void the payout, along with everything earned since.

A platform that can detect a breach in order to deny a payout could generally have detected it in real time and warned. The choice not to warn is the part worth noticing, because it means the trader's rule compliance is only ever measured when the firm has an incentive to find a breach.

Where people get fooled: treating the funded stage as the finish line and relaxing. The audit has not happened yet. Every trade taken before the first payout request is still live evidence, and unchecked assumptions about what was allowed do not expire — they accumulate.
Payout compliance review.usage: Refers to the retrospective audit a firm performs on the full account history when a withdrawal is requested.

Prop firm pass rate.long:
Two separate numbers matter here and they are routinely conflated. The first is the share of paying candidates who clear an evaluation. The second, much smaller, is the share who are ever actually paid.

Figures published in 2026 cluster around 5 to 10 percent clearing an evaluation. One dataset covering roughly 300,000 accounts reported about 14 percent reaching a funded account, and fewer than half of those receiving even one payout — leaving somewhere near 7 percent of all entrants paid anything at all. The reported failure pattern is consistent too: most accounts end in the first week, on the daily loss limit, rather than by running out of time short of a target.

These numbers deserve a heavy caveat. Almost all of them are published by firms that sell evaluations, or by affiliate sites paid to refer traders to them. Nobody with an incentive to understate is doing the counting.

Where people get fooled: reading a 7 percent figure as a skill filter, and assuming skill is what separates the 7 from the 93. Some of it is. But the same figure is also consistent with a business whose revenue is the fees, and a rulebook whose loss limits do most of the sorting before strategy has a chance to matter.
Prop firm pass rate.usage: Used for the proportion of evaluation buyers who become funded, and separately the proportion ever paid.

Prohibited strategy clause.long:
Every funded-account agreement names techniques that void the account. The usual list covers latency and arbitrage methods, tick scalping, reaction trading around restricted news, order copying between accounts or from a signal provider, and any pattern the firm characterises as exploiting its pricing rather than trading the market.

Two features of these clauses matter more than the list itself. The wording is typically broad and discretionary — phrases along the lines of exploiting inefficiencies, or trading not consistent with the spirit of the programme, which cannot be complied with precisely because they are not precise. And the judgement is made after the fact, by the firm, at the point of payout.

The consequence is that techniques which are entirely legal and unremarkable at an ordinary broker can void an account here. That is not necessarily bad faith; a firm carrying the other side of its own simulated fills has a genuine reason to exclude methods that target its pricing. But the party writing and interpreting the rules is also the party being traded against.

Where people get fooled: assuming that not appearing on the prohibited list means allowed. Discretionary wording means the list is a floor, not a boundary, and the interpretation that counts is the one applied when the withdrawal is requested.
Prohibited strategy clause.usage: Refers to the contract terms naming trading techniques that void a funded account.

Cross-account hedging.long:
The tactic is to buy two or more evaluations and take opposing positions across them, so that whichever way the market goes, one account shows the winning side and clears its target. The losing account is written off as the cost of the attempt.

On paper this converts a low-probability evaluation into an arithmetic problem about fees. In practice it is the single most anticipated form of gaming in the industry, and detection is close to universal — firms match execution timestamps, instruments, and position sizes across their own customer base, and increasingly share signals between firms.

It is also one of the most frequently cited grounds for voiding accounts and refusing payouts, including for traders who did not intend it. Two people trading the same well-known setup from the same public signal source can produce a pattern that resembles coordination closely enough to trigger a review.

Where people get fooled: assuming the hedge only has to survive until the payout. It does not — the compliance review looks at the whole history, and it looks hardest at accounts that have just become expensive. The tactic is most likely to be caught at exactly the moment it is supposed to pay off.
Cross-account hedging.usage: Describes taking opposing positions across multiple evaluations so one account is guaranteed to show a profit.

Payout cap.long:
A payout cap limits how much a funded account can withdraw. Some caps are per cycle — a maximum per payout window, or a percentage of the account's profit. Others are lifetime, bounding the total the account can ever pay out before it must be closed or reset.

A lifetime cap changes the arithmetic of the entire product. The evaluation fee, the reset fees and the loss limits are all uncapped on the downside, while the best possible outcome now has a ceiling on it. Expected value calculations built on an unbounded upside stop applying the moment such a cap exists, and the cap is usually the last term anyone reads.

Caps have been appearing more often as the industry matures. Apex introduced total-payout limits in the rulebook it launched in March 2026; because terms in this industry change frequently and without much notice, any specific figure quoted second-hand — including here — should be checked against the firm's current agreement rather than trusted.

Where people get fooled: comparing programmes on the profit split alone. A 90 percent split on a capped account can pay less in total than a 70 percent split on an uncapped one, and the split is the number on the advertisement while the cap is not.
Payout cap.usage: Refers to a ceiling on withdrawals from a funded account, whether per cycle or over its lifetime.

Overnight and weekend holding rule.long:
Many programmes restrict holding positions past the session close, into the weekend, or both. The restriction ranges from increased margin, through a requirement to be flat by a stated time, to outright prohibition with automatic liquidation of anything still open.

The reason is gap risk, and specifically whose gap risk it is. A position that gaps through its stop over a weekend produces a loss larger than the account's limit, and on a funded account that excess is the firm's problem rather than the trader's. Restricting the hold removes the exposure at its source.

The rule is most common on futures programmes, which sit on instruments with defined session breaks and meaningful overnight gaps. Apex prohibited overnight holding outright in its March 2026 rules; again, terms change often enough that this should be verified against the current agreement rather than assumed.

Where people get fooled: treating it as a formality and being liquidated automatically at the close, which on many programmes counts as a rule breach in its own right rather than a neutral flattening. It also quietly rules out entire categories of approach — anything swing-length or slower cannot be run on an account that must be flat every evening, regardless of whether the method works.
Overnight and weekend holding rule.usage: Refers to limits on carrying positions past the session close or across the weekend.

Prop firm regulatory status.long:
Most retail funded-account providers are not registered as financial firms in the jurisdictions they sell into. They are generally not brokers, not fund managers, and not registered with the NFA in the United States or authorised by the FCA in the United Kingdom. What they sell is usually described in their own terms as an educational service, a simulated trading product, or a skills assessment.

That framing is what keeps the model outside the registration regimes, and it is largely accurate on its own terms — a simulated account with a performance-linked prize genuinely is not a brokerage relationship. It also means the customer's protection is whatever the firm's agreement grants, with no regulator standing behind it and no compensation scheme if the firm fails or simply refuses to pay.

The sector's most prominent enforcement action illustrates how unsettled this is. The CFTC sued the operator of My Forex Funds in August 2023 with allegations including that accounts were simulated and the firm profited from customer losses. In May 2025 the case was dismissed with prejudice and the agency was sanctioned over its conduct — so those allegations were never established, and the episode is better read as evidence that the legal position is genuinely unresolved than as proof of anything about the industry.

Where people get fooled: reading marketing language about funding and capital as implying a regulated financial relationship. The money at risk is the fee, the counterparty is the firm, and the governing document is its terms of service.
Prop firm regulatory status.usage: Refers to the largely unregistered legal position of retail funded-account providers.

Account sharing.long:
Every firm prohibits letting another person trade an account, and prohibits running accounts on behalf of others. The stated reason is that the programme evaluates one identifiable individual, and an account traded by two people evaluates nobody.

Enforcement is technical and more thorough than most traders expect. Firms match device fingerprints, IP addresses, login timing, and execution patterns across their customer base, and identity is confirmed through KYC documentation before any payout is released. A mismatch between the person who traded and the person on the documents is straightforward to detect once anyone looks.

And, as with most rules in this industry, the looking happens at the payout review rather than in real time. An arrangement that ran unremarked for months is examined only when it becomes expensive.

Where people get fooled: informal versions that do not feel like sharing. Letting a friend place a trade while travelling, having a mentor take over during a drawdown, or a family member funding the fee and taking a cut all fall inside the prohibition as written. So does the reverse — buying an account someone else passed — which additionally means relying on a stranger's undetected breaches in a history that will eventually be audited in full.
Account sharing.usage: Refers to the prohibition on anyone other than the account holder trading a funded account.

Reading a prop firm rulebook.long:
Programmes are marketed on account size, profit split and fee. None of those three describe what the product actually is. A short list of structural questions does, and the answers are usually several clicks below the pricing page.

On losses: is the floor static or trailing? If trailing, does it move on unrealised intraday equity or only on the closing balance? Where does it lock, if it locks at all? Is there a separate daily limit, and is it measured on equity or on closed trades?

On profits: is there a consistency cap limiting what share of total profit one day may contribute? A minimum number of trading days? On payouts: how long is the first waiting period, is there a per-cycle or lifetime cap, and what documentation is required? On method: which techniques are named as prohibited, and how discretionary is that wording?

Where people get fooled: comparing programmes on the numbers both firms advertise, because those are the numbers chosen to be compared. Two accounts with identical headline size, split and drawdown can be entirely different products once the floor mechanics, the consistency cap and the payout ceiling are read. The questions above take about ten minutes and are the only part of the decision that is fully within the buyer's control.
Reading a prop firm rulebook.usage: Used for the structural questions that determine what a funded-account programme actually offers.
